en.title: Nationalities
en.goal: Say your nationality and other people's nationality, masculine and feminine.

lessons.nacionalidade-e-origem: German, Portuguese and asking where someone is from

phrases.scenario: Someone asks your nationality in a job interview. What do you say?

phrases.t: He is French, she is Spanish.
phrases.scenario: You're introducing two friends of different nationalities — a Frenchman and a Spanish woman. What do you say about them?
You've met someone new on a trip and want to know where they come from. What do you ask?
Someone asks where you come from, and you come from Portugal. What do you answer?

phrases.t: Nationality is written on the passport.

dialogue.title: Where are you from?
lines: No, I live in Portugal now.

etre-nationalite-vs-venir-de.title: "Je suis brésilienne" or "je viens du Brésil"?
etre-nationalite-vs-venir-de.body: Être + nationality talks about your identity (je suis brésilienne). Venir de + country talks about your origin / where you come from (je viens du Brésil). The two sentences say almost the same thing, but notice the preposition: du Brésil, de France, d'Espagne — it changes depending on the gender and the first letter of the country's name.

dou-viens-tu-wh-in-situ.title: "D'où viens-tu ?" also becomes "Tu es d'où ?"
dou-viens-tu-wh-in-situ.body: Notice that the dialogue you just read already uses the everyday form: Tu es d'où ? instead of "D'où viens-tu ?". In everyday speech, it's common to keep the normal subject-verb order and move the question word to the end. In the exercises here, keep using "D'où viens-tu ?" — it's the form the exercises ask for.

trueFalse.claim: This question is used to find out someone's name.
trueFalse.whyNote: Wrong — d'où viens-tu ? asks where the person comes FROM (viens = come), not their name. For a name you'd say "comment tu t'appelles ?".

review.why: EN adjectives have no gender, so I kept the (m.)/(f.) labels to preserve the masculine/feminine pair the lesson teaches (same for vocab[1]-[7])
literal 'venir de'; 'Where are you from?' is more natural but is used for 'Tu es d'où ?' to keep the lesson's contrast
feminine form of the FR sentence (brésilienne) is lost in EN
